Degrees, radians and the unit circle

Angles can be measured in degrees (360 in a full turn) or radians (2π in a full turn). Radians are the natural unit in calculus and physics. This converter works in both directions — you can type radians with π, such as 5pi/4 — and also places the angle on the unit circle, giving its quadrant, reference angle and exact sine, cosine and tangent for every multiple of 15°.

Try changing the input

Enter 30°, 150°, 210° and 330°. The reference angle stays 30°, so the values have the same size; only the signs change with the quadrant.

Formulas and key values

radians=degrees×π180degrees=radians×180π
θ0∘30∘=π645∘=π460∘=π390∘=π2
sin⁡θ01222321
cos⁡θ13222120
tan⁡θ03313undefined

On the unit circle (radius 1) the point at angle θ is (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ). The reference angle is the acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis; the quadrant decides the signs (sine is positive in quadrants I and II, cosine in I and IV, tangent in I and III).

Worked example

Convert 150° and find its trigonometric values

Step 1 — Convert

150∘×π180=5π6≈2.618 rad

Step 2 — Quadrant and reference angle

150° lies in quadrant II; its reference angle is 180∘−150∘=30∘.

Step 3 — Values with signs

sin⁡150∘=12,cos⁡150∘=−32,tan⁡150∘=−33

Assumptions, domain and rounding

  • Any real angle is accepted, including negative angles and angles larger than a full turn.
  • Exact values are given for multiples of 15°; other angles give rounded decimals.
  • A radian answer is shown as a multiple of π whenever it is a simple fraction of π.
